title: UCLA Nashaa, the Bollywood Dance Team Behind Netflix's Best of the Best
excerpt: The New York Times profiled UCLA's Bollywood-fusion team Nashaa through auditions and competitions; its captains and the film's costume designer explain what the Netflix comedy gets right.
body:
• UCLA Nashaa, the university's Bollywood-fusion dance team, is an inspiration for Netflix's comedy "Best of the Best," released September 18, 2026.
  • The New York Times profiled Nashaa through auditions, late-night rehearsals and competitions, and UCLA Newsroom highlighted the coverage on September 28.
  • In the film, the fictional UCLA Agni stands in for real collegiate teams; co-captains say its parking-garage practices and costume choices ring true.
  • For diaspora students, Nashaa is a concrete way to connect with South Asian culture on campus — dance, in one member's words quoted by UCLA, is how many connect.

For South Asian students at UCLA, the road to a national dance championship now runs through Netflix. The streaming comedy "Best of the Best," written by Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam and directed by Lena Khan, follows best friends Maya and Anjali, played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, as they try to join a collegiate Bollywood dance team at UCLA. Behind the fictional team, UCLA Agni, stands a real one: UCLA Nashaa, the university's Bollywood-fusion dance team.

The real team behind the film

UCLA Newsroom reported on September 28 that the New York Times had profiled Nashaa, documenting the team through auditions, late-night rehearsals and competitions. The university said the piece explores how the team gives South Asian students a way to connect with their culture and build community. That framing matches what Nashaa members told the Daily Bruin. Pranav Bhramasandra, a co-captain and second-year computer science and linguistics student, said seeing a movie about his college dance team was very exciting, and that its depiction of students practicing in a parking garage resonated with him.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=D_H0qs5heRY

"For a lot of South Asians, dance is the way we connect."

— UCLA Nashaa member, quoted by UCLA Newsroom from the New York Times profile

Costumes that have to move

The Daily Bruin's interview with costume designer Liz Vastola shows how seriously the production treated the circuit it was portraying. Vastola, known for work on "Daredevil" and "Twisted Metal," said she immersed herself in South Asian fashion, drawing on choreographers including Usha Jey and Parris Goebel, brands such as NorBlack NorWhite, and the book "The Offbeat Sari." For a Bollywood wedding sequence, her team deflated the skirts of two bridal lehengas by removing layers and replaced beading with sequins in places so the actors could actually dance in them.

Nashaa makes the same calculations in real life. Co-captain Saanvi Thattai, a second-year human biology and society student, told the Daily Bruin the team styles pieces around the dance style of each set: more comfort and lightweight pieces two years ago, and more pants-and-shirts costumes last year when the set leaned less Bollywood and more hip-hop and bhangra.

A circuit bigger than one campus

Collegiate Bollywood-fusion is a national competitive circuit, with teams blending Bollywood movement with hip-hop, bhangra, salsa and ballet and travelling to face rivals from other universities. The film builds its rivalry around a fictional USC team, but the structure — brutal tryouts, captains setting costume and choreography, a national title at stake — is the structure Nashaa members describe. Bhramasandra found some details dramatized, including arguments over lead dancer positions, while calling other parts, and the characters' casual outfits, realistic.

What it means for the diaspora

"Best of the Best" is streaming worldwide on Netflix now, so diaspora families can watch the film and then look up Nashaa's own competition performances online. For parents who grew up with Bollywood and children growing up in Los Angeles, the team offers a shared reference point: a campus institution where South Asian culture is not an elective or a festival day, but a year-round competitive commitment.

What's next

Nashaa returns to the audition-and-competition cycle that the Times documented, while the film's makers have framed it as a tribute drawn from the writers' own college dance experience. Whether it brings new audiences — and new recruits — to collegiate Bollywood-fusion will show in this season's tryouts.
